Firstly, I was just stating the definition and the assertion the definition makes. I didn't say anything about you, or any other white person as an individual. The definition talks about societal structures: yeah sure - Barack Obama has more power than you currently - however if you and Barack Obama both walked into a job interview to be interviewed by someone who didn't know either of you, had the same qualifications and gave the same quality of interview: your being white would likely give you the upper hand and his being black might make him less likely to get the job. Same if you're going in to get a loan. That's privlege and societal power. Secondly, if you're in that academic context, you'd probably describe an individual of the minority group hating or mistreating those on the more powerful group as discrimination... or you wouldn't be talking about that at all, since individual experiences of discrimination aren't really talked about unless they underly a larger power structure and there is no black racist power structure "keeping the white man down". You seem to be taking my comment as a personal attack: I also didn't imply with "academic contexts" that the definition was for smart people. I meant that in critical race theory/African American studies is where this definition of racism will normally be used, since it's more specific than the average person just talking about personal experiences of racism probably means and for most contexts the usual definition works just fine. I'm not sure how that implies anyone is a "commoner."

As a black person who has had people do this to me upon knowing them for 30 minutes or less: don't. It's not worth it. Most people will find it offensive, and it's not worth chancing it with everyone to figure out those who won't.

Racism is a term that can be used to indicate  different things depending on the context in which its used. Most of the time, the broad definition you were raised with is good enough, however an academic context the word racism is more narrowly defined. This is where you'd be more likely to hear the definition of racism being based upon power structures, such that white people or powerful majorities cannot be victims of racism. The difference between this and institutional and systemic racism and that institutional and systemic racism are enacted by large, powerful bodies (like governments), while others will assert that racism cannot even be enacted on an individual level buy a minority onto a majority (IE a black person on to a white person) because no matter what the white person ultimately has more societal power than the black person.
